chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Welcome back to Medical Engineering and today we want to continue our little excursion through

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the theory but you'll see that we'll get much more applied in the next couple of videos

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: because in the next two videos we want to talk about actual 2D signal processing and

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the first thing that we want to look at is an introduction into 2D image processing and

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: we'll start with simple operations and expand them to linear system theory and filters

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and then in a second step we will look into non-linear systems.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So I hope you enjoy the 2D image processing with me.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So here we are at with the Medical Engineering Systems and today the topic will be image processing.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So let's have a look at the basics of image processing.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Now an image is essentially a 2D function and you can think of the image as a function that

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: essentially is on a grid space where you could say essentially every column and every row

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: is a function or a signal as we've discussed earlier and now we have to expand the space

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and to be able to work with these 2D signals.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: On the right hand side you see an visualization and you can see here that we have the red function

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: which is essentially one column and this is a sequence of values that you can see here

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: plotted and we also have the blue function which is essentially one row and it's again

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: a sequence of values.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Together these grey values here in this example form a 2D image.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Now you see the lady here that is actually Lennar and this is one of the first images

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: that was used for image processing.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: It actually originates from a magazine that was published in November 1972.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So at that time there were not so many scanners and digital images available.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: It happened that one of those images were scanned so they took a subsection of one of

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the largest images that they could find in the magazine.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: They scanned it and actually this image became kind of iconic and has been used in image

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: processing over and over again.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So Lennar became extremely popular and she has also been invited although she didn't

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: know about her fans in the image processing community so she has been invited actually

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: to a couple of conferences and she is still being welcomed warmheartedly on various conferences

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and today people still use this image in order to test their algorithms.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Well actually there's many other image sets that people experiment with now but sometimes

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: for nostalgic reasons this image is still being used.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Note that only this subsection that we are showing here is being used and the full image is not

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: being commonly used in the image processing community.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So just that you don't get the wrong impression it was just one of the images that was lying

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: around and that they had access to and they decided to use the subsection of the image.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: What's the digital image?

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So let's go back and think of our function space and what you can see here is a highly magnified

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: image so this is just showing a couple of black and gray dots and what you see here is that

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: essentially every color, every shade of gray is associated to a value.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So the gray that you can see here it's a light gray so it's associated to the value 200

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and the dark color, the black is associated in this example to the color 35.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So essentially every shade of gray is associated to a number and this number originated from

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: a sampling process as we discussed in the last video.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Obviously these are the images that are used to introduce image processing what we will work with

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: much more frequently are of course medical images and one thing that is very peculiar about

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: medical images is that they often have more gray values, more shades of gray, that you can actually

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: show at the same time on your monitor and actually more than you can perceive.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So the human visual system can approximately differentiate 256 different shades of gray.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: You cannot differentiate more or the average human being cannot differentiate more and if you

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: display them you will see that they appear as a continuous color gradient or gray value gradient

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: on your screen. So in order to be able to visualize all of the information that is in the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: medical image we have to use tricks. One trick that you could come up with is using different

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: gamma values and you see them here we can do a gamma correction which is a non-linear scaling

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: of the gray values and if we would do so we would be able to focus more on the skull or on the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: brain and change the color values. This however is not so frequently used in medical imaging.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: What is much more common is so called window leveling. So here we have an example of a

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: CT image and we know that Huntsville units denoted as HU here are associated to different materials

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and on the left hand side and the right hand side you see exactly the same image but displayed

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: in a different window level. So minus a thousand Huntsville units is air and plus a thousand Huntsville

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: units is bone or contrast agent and you see here that we can visualize all of the materials on the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: left hand side ranging from air up to contrast agent that you can see in the heart and the bones

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and then on the right hand side image water-rich materials such as water and soft tissues are

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: around zero Huntsville units and if we pick a fresh out that is above zero Huntsville units only

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the contrast agent and the bone will be visible. So what you see in this image is the contrast agent

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: in the heart and the bones and you see that this is an interventional scan so there is still some

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: residual artifact that you see at the bottom of the scan and this was caused by a truncation

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: at the end of the volume. So also sometimes these scans have associated artifacts and you have

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: to know about the problems that can arise in the scanning process in order not to misread

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the information here. So for sure there is no ring-like bone structure at the bottom of the scan

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: here but this is artificially created by the reconstruction method and if you're reading these

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: images if you're interpreting these images you have to know about this. Obviously there is a

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: wide range of variations that you can pick for windowing and thresholding and this is why I have a

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: short video where we are playing with the window and threshold in different settings.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So what you see is that the image is actually composed of different grey values.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Now what I'm showing here is called a histogram and a histogram is essentially a kind of

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: probability distribution because you count the frequency, the occurrence of every grey value.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So on the left hand side example we have grey values from 0 to 255 so 256 different shades of grain

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and you can see on the y-axis how often that respective color or grey value appeared in the image.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So the histogram doesn't contain the spatial information anymore but it tells you which grey value

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: occurs how frequently. Now if we change the window and level what we're essentially doing is

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: we're adjusting the histogram and here on the right hand side you can see a rescaling of the same

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: histogram to only 16 bins. So here we have pooled neighboring grey values in order to reduce

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the number of grey values in that particular image. Obviously this would have a large impact

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: on the displayed image and you could immediately see that I adjusted the number of grey values.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So this is something that we want to in the following. Now let's go back to our example image.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So here you see our famous learner and if you look at the associated histogram here on the right

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: hand side you see that actually not all of the 256 grey values actually appear in the image.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So you see that there is a short area with very low grey values and very high grey values where the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: frequency is 0 so they never appear in the image. And you can see also that our learner,

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: well the image impression is kind of okay but she could use a little bit more contrast right.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So this is where histogram equalization comes in. In histogram equalization the idea is that we want

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: to optimally use all of the associated grey values. What we're doing here is we're showing the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: cumulative density function which means that we're essentially computing the integral over the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: histogram. So at every point in the cumulative density function I am showing the addition of all

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the values from the zero of bin to the current bin. So this can be computed essentially with a

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: for loop where you then add up all of the previous values and write them into the respective bin.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Now if I normalize this with the total number of pixels in the image you will see that we get

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: values between zero and one. If you look at the left hand side image you see the cumulative

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: density function of our original image. And you can also see that plateaus at the very low values

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and at the very high values where we don't have any change in grey values anymore because these

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: grey values simply do not occur in the image. Now the idea of histogram equalization is that you

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: transform this cumulative density function on the left into the one on the right. So we want to

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: linearize the entire cumulative density function which essentially means that we try to achieve

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: a more or less uniform distribution of the grey values. There is algorithms to do so and in

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: particular they then introduce small gaps in the histogram such that all of the grey values

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: are being used. So you could say this is very similar to what we are achieving when we apply

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the window leveling. Now here you can see a histogram that has been equalized and now the contrast

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: of the image has been improved and you can see that our lowest grey value is now really zero

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and the highest grey value is really 255. Let's compare the two images and here you can clearly see that

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the right hand side image has a much better contrast than the left hand side image.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Good so these are the very basics of image processing and now we want to go ahead and look what we

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: can achieve with linear systems theory. And one thing that can be very nicely achieved is

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: computing derivatives. Now a derivative of a function if you look at the definition this is

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: essentially the limit of the function plus a small value at the position x and then you subtract

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the original value at position x from that and divide by the small value h.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: If you now have the limit of h towards zero you get the continuous derivative.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Now the problem that we have is that we are in a discrete space. In a discrete space we cannot

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: assign values of h that are lower than one because they would be zero and then our whole computation

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: would simply collapse to zero. So what we do is we then choose different variants of doing a

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: single as step size of one and then you come up with the solution shown here at the bottom.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So you can for example take the value of one for h then you add one to the function f of x

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and subtract f of x from that. This would be the forward difference. There is the backward

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: difference where you set h to minus one so you subtract one then the two flip and you have f of

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: x minus f of x minus one. So the problem with those two approaches is that you're essentially

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: computing the derivative at the position x plus 0.5. So you are kind of shifting the coordinate

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: system and you wouldn't be in the original coordinate system which is the reason why very frequently

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: there's also central differences and the central difference then simply takes the pixel on the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: right hand side and subtracts the pixel on the left hand side of the current position of the image.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: This is interesting because it allows us to compute image derivatives. Now why would we be

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: interested in image derivatives? Well let's look at an example and here you can see that the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: derivatives in x and y direction and what you see very nicely here is that the edges pop up.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So edges in our image are locations of very high gradients. So here you have either in x or y

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: directions very high derivatives. So one idea for example to detect edges is to compute the derivative

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and x and y direction and then compute the magnitude of the two. So because you have a two-dimensional

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: function you will be introducing a gradient that is also two-dimensional because you compute

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the derivatives in x and y direction and then you take the norm for example the l2 norm of this

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: gradient and this way you can determine the magnitude and detect edges. Also interesting is that

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: you can also compute the direction and then you could compute the angle of the edges which then

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: allows you also detect edges of a certain orientation. So this is a very very common application

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: for linear systems and a good way of how we can actually compute edges in an image.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: This brings us back to image filtering and linear systems theory. So you remember that a filter

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: can be applied to an image and this filter has very similar properties as we already have discussed

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: in the 1D case. So the filters are linear and they are shift invariant. So this is a linear

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: shift invariant system which means that it can be entirely described by convolution.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: And therefore we will need a 2D convolution and now you can see here that we have some function

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: k which is filter kernel and the filter kernel now takes the role of the impulse response

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: that we talked about earlier in our systems theory. So now we have suddenly 2D impulse responses

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and these can be written up in a discrete fashion and then we end up with filter kernels.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: For some functions they can be described in a very compact way such as for the derivative

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: we've seen that every point of the image we essentially have to take the left neighbor and the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: right neighbor subtract the two from each other and then we get exactly the derivative in that

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: particular direction. So that's interesting because we've just seen that computing a derivative

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: can be performed by convolution and for a derivative we can determine a kernel that is performing

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the derivative. So this means that computing derivatives is something that can be explained

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: by a linear shift invariant system. So that's actually pretty useful and you will see that

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: throughout your studies this will have many many applications and it's also very useful for

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: example for solving partial differential equations. So you will see this will come up over and

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: over again in your studies. Here we will now only stick to the discrete version and the nice

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: thing with the discrete version is that we can write these up as these filter kernels and you will

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: see that this then takes the form of very small masks for several filters such as the derivative

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: filter. A side remark of course linear system theory applies and also the fundamental properties

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: apply which means that if you have a filter kernel and you convert it into Fourier domain

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and you have the image and you convert it to 2D Fourier domain then you just have to multiply

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the two point wise and convert back and you do exactly a convolution. Now for the simple filters

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: that we have here in this set of slides this would be rather excessive because typically the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: kernels are very small they are like one by three or three by three or five by five these are

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: really compact kernels and there it doesn't make sense to compute the complete Fourier transform

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: but sometimes you have kernels with very large extent in spatial domain and there it makes sense to

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: make use of the Fourier properties here. Also you will see that the 2D Fourier space is something

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: that comes up in this class again and again. Now what's actually a 2D Fourier space?

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: You remember that when we are computing the 1D Fourier transform we essentially take a signal

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: of a fixed frequency and then we multiply it point wise with the signal that we want to process

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: some everything up and we get the coefficient for that particular frequency.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Now in the 2D case this is slightly different because now our 2D waves have to be described also

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: in 2D which means that it's not just the frequency of the wave but they also have an orientation.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So they are essentially sine and cosine wave fronts that have a particular orientation and you

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: can see that they are printed here the base functions on the set of slides and they vary in orientation

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and in frequency so the frequency you can determine by looking essentially from one value to the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: next value so that's the wavelength and this is associated to one over the wavelength will give

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: you the frequency. So what you see in this image now is that we can compute one point in the 2D

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Fourier transform by taking one of the wave fronts that you see with different orientations

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: multiplying the entire image point wise with this wave front and summing everything up.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: This will then give you exactly one point in 2D Fourier space. So this is actually quite expensive

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: to compute because we have to instantiate all those wave fronts then we have to multiply them

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: point wise with the image and add everything up and then you just got one point in the 2D Fourier

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: space. Also see that the farther you go away from the center the shorter the wavelength gets

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and the higher the frequency and the closer you get to the center the longer the wavelength

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and the lower the frequency. Also note that depending on the orientation the direction that you're at

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the orientation of the wave front changes. Now if you look at this image then you can also see very

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: easily that if you would be rotating the image then essentially you're also rotating the 2D

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Fourier space. So if you have a rotation in the spatial domain this will also be a rotation in 2D

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Fourier space. That's quite interesting to see right? So keep that in mind if you want to go to

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Fourier space you have to compute those wave fronts multiply them point wise with each other

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: and add them up and if you want to go back it's the same as we discussed earlier. So you take

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the coefficient at that particular point in the 2D Fourier transform you multiply this with the

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: complete 2D wave front and then you repeat that for all of the points in the 2D Fourier space and

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: add everything up and this way you get the original image again.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: Okay so let's return to our example and now let's discuss the filter kernel. So the filter kernel

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: here for the derivative filter of the central difference is simply this 3 by 1 matrix. So you

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: simply have the derivative with respect to x written up here so you take minus 1 times f of x

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: minus 1 y plus 0 times f of xy plus 1 time f of x plus 1 y and this is now the impulse response

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the filter kernel that you have to convolve with in order to generate a derivative in x direction.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: So for computing the derivative in y direction you have to transpose the kernel and then you get

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: the solution here on the top right which will be able to compute the derivative in x direction.

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: By the way there is also second order derivatives and the second order derivatives can be

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: determined also in discrete fashion and here this is simply the convolution of the kernel

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
chunks.text: with itself. So if you convolve the x kernel with itself you get exactly the 1 minus 2 1 and if

chunks.title: image_processing_high_res
